title: Why music
hook: raga is theology: the Word must be felt, not only read

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Granth's languages: Punjabi, Persian, Braj and the speech of the saints, in one alphabet. Your line was many tongues, one script. Did you hear a borrowed word somewhere? Day one thousand four hundred thirteen.

The harmonium wheezes into its first note before anyone sings a word. Then the tabla comes in, soft at first, and a voice lifts a line from the Guru Granth Sahib, and the people sitting on the floor sing it back. In the gurdwara, the hymns are sung. A visitor might wonder why. If the words are holy, why not just read them out, clearly, so nobody misses a syllable? Why the melody, the rhythm, the repeated line? The Sikh answer is not that music makes the words prettier. It's closer to this: some things have to reach you through the ear and the chest before they reach the head.
screen: `THE HARMONIUM, THE TABLA, A VOICE.` → `WHY NOT JUST READ IT?` → `THROUGH THE EAR AND THE CHEST.`

segments.voice: First, look at how the book is built. After the opening prayers, the Granth is arranged by raga. Each hymn sits under a heading that names its musical mode before it names the Guru who wrote it. The book is ordered like a songbook, by mood, not by date or author. A raga isn't just a tune. It's a mood, a color, a time of day, and the hymn was meant to arrive inside it. Second, the first musician. Tradition says Guru Nanak traveled with a Muslim companion, Bhai Mardana, who played the rabab, a stringed instrument. The janamsakhis, the old story collections, tell of Nanak asking Mardana to play, and the hymn coming as song. From the start, as Sikhs tell it, the Word came with music under it. Third, the word for this singing: kirtan, singing the praise of God. Guru Arjan, in Raag Maru, says that in this dark age kirtan is foremost. Not a decoration. Foremost. Fourth, why it matters. You can read a line about longing and understand it. Sung in a raga made for longing, you meet it differently: in the breath, in the pause before the line comes back. Many Sikh teachers speak of the Word needing to be felt, not only parsed. Music slows you down to the speed of the hymn. It makes you repeat. It lets a room of strangers carry the same line together. A spoken sentence can slip past. A sung line comes around again.
screen: `THE GRANTH IS ORDERED BY RAGA.` · `MARDANA'S RABAB, TRADITION SAYS.` · `KIRTAN IS FOREMOST.` · `A MELODY STAYS.` · then, large: `FELT, NOT JUST READ.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen and feel. If you can, play one recording of kirtan, any shabad, quietly. If you can't, just listen to the sounds around you. Settle, and breathe. Don't try to follow every word. Let the sound land somewhere in your body first: the chest, the throat, behind the eyes. Notice where it lands. When a line comes back around, let it come back. If you'd like to, hum along on one long note, low and easy. If you pray, the listening can be the prayer. The bell holds the time.
Why music. Because the Granth is a songbook ordered by raga, and kirtan, singing the praise, carries the Word into the body. Today's word.
Your line: felt, not just read. Today, take one sentence that matters to you and hum it, or say it slowly with a rhythm, instead of only reading it. Day one thousand four hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: In gurdwaras, the hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib are sung as kirtan, usually with harmonium and tabla, in the raga named at the head of each hymn, and the congregation often sings the refrain together.
